children: Iron ore prices rose for a fourth straight session on Tuesday, helped by falling shipments and hopes of demand picking up seasonally in top consumer China, although elevated portside stocks and thin steel margins limited gains.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
rose 0.61% to 739 yuan ($110.12) a metric ton by 0143 GMT. It touched its highest level since July 28 at 745 yuan earlier in the session.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was up 0.33% at $100.65 a ton, as of 0133 GMT, after hitting its strongest level since June 17 at $101.3 earlier.

Market sentiment was bolstered as iron ore shipments from major suppliers Australia and Brazil to China slid 7.7% from the prior week to 23.03 million tons, as of September 6, according to Reuters calculations based on data from consultancy Mysteel.
Moreover, the production suspension at Brazilian miner Usiminas
due to weaker ore prices and sharply higher freight costs raised concerns among some traders over whether more small-scale miners will follow.
Also supporting prices of the key steelmaking ingredient was hope of rising demand as steelmakers started to restock for the upcoming week-long National Day holiday break in early October.

However, elevated portside stocks — standing at 152.63 million tons on September 4, according to data from consultancy Steelhome — limited ore price upside, analysts at broker Zhengxin Futures said in a note.
Separately, the Dalian bourse will adjust the price limit range and trading margins for iron ore futures contracts to 6% and 8% from the previous 9% and 11%.
